case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the six-year statute of limitations for an APA challenge to an agency rule begins to run when the rule is issued or only when the plaintiff is first injured/adversely affected by the rule.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2401(a) (six-year limit for civil actions against the United States; claim 'first accrues') and 5 U.S.C. § 702 (APA cause of action for a person who suffers 'legal wrong' or is 'adversely affected or aggrieved').
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Corner Post argues that an APA claim does not 'first accrue' under § 2401(a) until the plaintiff has a complete and enforceable claim—i.e., when the challenged rule actually causes the plaintiff to suffer a legal wrong or be adversely affected/aggrieved under § 702. Because some regulated parties (including newly formed businesses) may not exist or may not be harmed at the time a rule is promulgated, starting the clock at issuance would bar suits before they can be brought, undermining judicial review and allowing unlawful rules to become effectively unreviewable for later-injured parties. Petitioner and supporting amici emphasize traditional accrual principles (injury-based accrual), the APA’s text tying reviewability to injury, and fairness/constitutional avoidance concerns if limitations run before a claimant can sue.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Board argues that for facial challenges to agency rules, the claim 'first accrues' when the agency issues the final rule because that is the definitive agency action and the time when the rule becomes legally operative. Starting the limitations clock at issuance promotes repose, regulatory certainty, and efficient administration by preventing perpetual vulnerability of long-settled rules. Respondent also points to the dominant circuit approach (including the Eighth Circuit below) that treats promulgation as the accrual date for APA challenges to regulations, and contends that affected parties had earlier opportunities to litigate and that equitable doctrines (like tolling) are limited and were not warranted here.
key_precedents: Circuit split referenced in the Question Presented: Eighth Circuit and five other circuits (issuance-based accrual) vs. Sixth Circuit (injury-based accrual for later-injured plaintiffs) (specific case names not provided in the supplied documents)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s repose-and-administrability concern remains the strongest point for Respondent, but it cannot justify reading § 2401(a)’s “right of action first accrues” to run from promulgation for plaintiffs who were not yet “adversely affected or aggrieved” under APA § 702—doing so would function as an unexpressed statute of repose that can expire before any complete and present cause of action exists. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Bay Area Laundry’s ordinary accrual rule, reinforced by Crown Coat’s linkage between accrual and the availability of judicial review, underscores that a claim does not accrue before a plaintiff can sue. To preserve institutional legitimacy and stability without rewriting the statute, I would adopt the minimalist path Justice Kagan suggests: limit the holding to later-injured plaintiffs and leave broader questions about facial pre-enforcement challenges and remedial scope for another day. On that narrow ground, text and precedent still point to injury-based accrual for these plaintiffs.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s repose-and-administrability concern is the strongest argument for the other side, but it cannot overcome the text Congress enacted: § 2401(a) runs from when the “right of action first accrues,” and ordinary legal meaning ties accrual to when the plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action, not merely when the agency acted. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, pegging accrual to promulgation for later-injured parties would convert a limitations provision into an atextual statute of repose that can expire before APA § 702’s “adversely affected or aggrieved” condition—and even Article III injury—exists. Crown Coat’s linkage between accrual and the availability of judicial review further confirms that a claim cannot accrue when no one in the plaintiff’s position could yet sue. Stability interests are real, but under an originalist and textualist approach they must be addressed through Congress or remedial limits, not by rewriting “accrues” to mean “promulgation.”

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest Respondent argument remains my own: § 2401(a) should be read to promote repose by starting the clock at promulgation to prevent perpetual destabilization of settled regulations. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, the statutory text—“right of action first accrues”—tracks ordinary accrual principles (a complete and present claim), and Crown Coat reinforces that accrual turns on when judicial review is available, not simply when the agency acted. Tying accrual to promulgation for later-injured plaintiffs would effectively convert § 2401(a) into a statute of repose that can expire before APA § 702’s “adversely affected or aggrieved” condition (and Article III injury) exists, a result I cannot justify as a textualist absent clearer congressional direction. The practical stability concerns can be mitigated, as Justice Kagan suggests, through as-applied framing and remedial limits rather than by rewriting “accrues.”

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s repose-and-administrability concern is the strongest point for Respondent, but it asks us to treat § 2401(a) as a statute of repose without clear congressional language—an approach that would bar later-injured parties before they can satisfy APA § 702’s “adversely affected or aggrieved” requirement or Article III injury. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, our ordinary accrual rule (Bay Area Laundry) ties “first accrues” to when the plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action, and Crown Coat reinforces that accrual tracks the moment judicial review becomes available. I also agree with Justice Thomas that calling § 702 merely a “who may sue” provision does not solve the problem that no cognizable claim exists at promulgation for those not yet injured. Pragmatically, any stability interests can be protected through as-applied framing and remedial tailoring rather than extinguishing access to review for new entrants and vulnerable litigants who could not realistically sue at promulgation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s repose/administrability concern remains the strongest argument for Respondent, but it still depends on treating § 2401(a)’s “right of action first accrues” as triggered by promulgation—an interpretation that departs from the ordinary accrual rule requiring a complete and present cause of action. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, that move effectively converts a limitations provision into a statute of repose that can expire before any plaintiff is “adversely affected or aggrieved” under APA § 702, and Crown Coat reinforces that accrual tracks when judicial review is available to the claimant. Stability interests are real, but as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch note, they are better handled through remedial tailoring and an as-applied posture rather than rewriting “accrues” to mean “when the agency acted.” No circuit practice about “facial” challenges supplies the clear textual signal needed to displace that baseline accrual understanding.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s repose-and-administrability point is the strongest counter, but it cannot justify reworking § 2401(a)’s ordinary accrual language into a promulgation-triggered statute of repose. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, a “right of action first accrues” when the plaintiff has a complete and present claim, and APA § 702’s “adversely affected or aggrieved” requirement confirms that many later-injured parties had no cognizable claim at promulgation—so nothing existed to accrue. Crown Coat (invoked by the Chief) strengthens that conclusion by tying accrual to when judicial review is available to the claimant, not simply when the government acts. Stability concerns are real, but—as Justice Kagan notes—they are better handled through remedial limits and as-applied posture than by reading “accrues” contrary to its established legal meaning.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s repose-and-administrability concern is the strongest counterweight, but it cannot justify construing § 2401(a)’s “right of action first accrues” to begin at promulgation for plaintiffs who were not yet “adversely affected or aggrieved” under APA § 702. As the Chief Justice notes, that reading would function as an atextual statute of repose, potentially expiring claims before judicial review is even available—something Crown Coat’s linkage between accrual and review-availability cuts against. I agree with Justice Thomas that ordinary accrual principles (a complete and present cause of action) are the best fit with the text and our precedents, and stability interests should be handled through remedial tailoring rather than by rewriting accrual. On an institutionalist approach, that narrower, injury-based accrual rule preserves both legality and legitimacy by keeping the courthouse open to later-injured parties without adopting a sweeping theory that insulates unlawful rules from any review.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s repose/administrability argument is the strongest point for Respondent, but it still requires treating § 2401(a)’s “right of action first accrues” as a promulgation-triggered statute of repose—despite Congress using classic accrual language that, as the Chief Justice notes, ordinarily turns on a plaintiff’s complete and present cause of action. As Justice Thomas emphasizes, APA § 702’s “adversely affected or aggrieved” requirement means many later-injured parties have no cognizable claim at promulgation, so starting (and potentially ending) the six-year clock then would bar suit before any statutory right of action exists. Crown Coat’s linkage of accrual to when judicial review is available reinforces that reading and makes the promulgation rule hard to defend on textualist/originalist terms. Stability concerns can be addressed through remedial tailoring and as-applied framing, but not by rewriting “accrues” to mean “when the agency acted.”

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s repose-and-administrability concern is the strongest counterweight, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 2401(a)’s “right of action first accrues” tracks the ordinary rule that accrual requires a complete and present cause of action—something a later-injured plaintiff lacks until they are “adversely affected or aggrieved” under APA § 702. Reading accrual as pegged to promulgation would function as an atextual statute of repose that can expire before Article III injury and statutory review entitlement exist, a procedural unfairness I cannot accept absent a clear congressional signal. Crown Coat’s linkage between accrual and the availability of judicial review reinforces that we should not start the clock when no claimant can yet sue. Stability interests are real, but as Justice Kagan notes they are better handled through remedial tailoring and as-applied limitations rather than barring later-injured parties from any review.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 2401(a) provides that the six-year period runs when a claim “first accrues,” and ordinary accrual principles treat a claim as accruing only when the plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action—i.e., when the plaintiff is actually “adversely affected or aggrieved” under APA § 702. Reading accrual to occur at rule promulgation for all plaintiffs would effectively convert § 2401(a) into a statute of repose for later-injured parties, barring suits before they can be filed and undermining the APA’s injury-based cause of action recognized alongside finality in Lujan v. National Wildlife Federation, 497 U.S. 871, 882–83 (1990). That injury-based reading is also consistent with the Court’s distinction between statutes of limitations and repose in CTS Corp. v. Waldburger, 573 U.S. 1, 7–8 (2014), while still permitting narrow, as-applied review that minimizes disruption to settled regulatory regimes. To preserve institutional legitimacy and avoid creating an atextual repose period, the limitations clock should begin when the plaintiff is first injured by the rule, not merely when the agency issues it.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 28 U.S.C. § 2401(a) provides that the six-year period runs after the claim “first accrues,” and under the ordinary meaning of accrual at the Founding and in our early cases, a claim accrues when a plaintiff has a complete and enforceable cause of action—i.e., when suit may first be brought. The APA confirms that understanding: 5 U.S.C. § 702 authorizes suit only by a person who has suffered a “legal wrong” or is “adversely affected or aggrieved,” which cannot occur for a later-created or later-injured regulated party at the time of promulgation. Reading § 2401(a) to start at issuance would force the limitations period to run before the plaintiff can sue, an atextual result inconsistent with the statute’s language and the traditional accrual rule reflected in Rice v. United States and applied in Crown Coat Front Co. v. United States (where accrual tied to the point judicial review became available). Therefore, the better textual reading is that an APA claim accrues when the plaintiff is first injured/adversely affected by the rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2401(a) provides that the six-year period runs from when the claim "first accrues," and for a facial APA challenge to a final rule that moment is when the agency completes the definitive, legally operative action—promulgation and publication of the rule. Treating issuance as accrual best serves repose, regulatory certainty, and administrability, avoiding a regime in which long-settled rules remain perpetually vulnerable whenever a new entrant later experiences downstream effects. While Bay Area Laundry states the general rule that accrual occurs when a plaintiff has a "complete and present cause of action," 522 U.S. 192, 201 (1997), § 702’s injury requirement is properly understood as a standing/zone-of-interests gatekeeping principle rather than a device to restart § 2401(a) for facial attacks on regulations. The prevailing circuit approach recognizing promulgation-based accrual for facial challenges better accords with the practical consequences of nationwide regulation and the need for stable enforcement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2401(a) runs from when a plaintiff’s “right of action first accrues,” and under traditional accrual principles a claim is not “complete and present” until the plaintiff can file suit and obtain relief. Bay Area Laundry & Dry Cleaning Pension Tr. Fund v. Ferbar Corp. confirms that limitations generally begin only when the cause of action has ripened, and 5 U.S.C. § 702 ties an APA cause of action to when a person suffers a “legal wrong” or is “adversely affected or aggrieved,” not merely when the agency issues a rule. Starting the clock at promulgation would bar suits by later-injured or newly formed parties before they have standing, undermining access to judicial review and entrenching potentially unlawful rules against vulnerable and less-resourced litigants. Nothing in § 2401(a) clearly displaces the ordinary injury-based accrual rule, and fairness and practical consequences favor allowing later-injured plaintiffs their own six-year window from first injury.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2401(a) bars suit unless filed within six years after the “right of action first accrues,” and our usual rule is that accrual occurs when the plaintiff has a “complete and present cause of action”—i.e., when it can file suit and obtain relief. Bay Area Laundry confirms that presumption absent a clear congressional instruction to the contrary, and nothing in § 2401(a) resets accrual to the date of the government’s rulemaking rather than the plaintiff’s legally cognizable injury. The APA likewise ties who may sue to injury: § 702 authorizes review only for a person who suffers a “legal wrong” or is “adversely affected or aggrieved,” which supports an injury-based start date so that later-injured parties are not time-barred before they can sue. While the government’s repose interests are weighty, they are better addressed through doctrines about the scope of relief and workability in particular cases, not by rewriting “accrues” to mean “when the agency acted.”

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2401(a) starts the six-year clock when a claim “first accrues,” and this Court has long understood accrual to occur only when the plaintiff has a “complete and present cause of action”—that is, when the plaintiff can file suit and obtain relief. Bay Area Laundry & Dry Cleaning Pension Tr. Fund v. Ferbar Corp. of Cal., 522 U.S. 192, 201 (1997). The APA likewise authorizes suit only for a person who has suffered a “legal wrong” or is “adversely affected or aggrieved,” 5 U.S.C. § 702, so a plaintiff not yet injured by a rule lacks a ripe, enforceable claim and cannot be forced to litigate before Article III standing exists. Reading § 2401(a) to run from issuance would allow limitations to expire before any suit may be brought, atextually insulating unlawful rules from judicial review for later-injured parties and undermining the separation-of-powers design that assigns courts the job of saying what the law is.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 2401(a) bars suits filed more than six years after the right of action “first accrues,” and under this Court’s traditional accrual rule a claim accrues when the plaintiff has a “complete and present cause of action”—that is, when the plaintiff can file suit and obtain relief. Bay Area Laundry & Dry Cleaning Pension Tr. Fund v. Ferbar Corp. confirms that accrual ordinarily turns on the plaintiff’s ability to sue, not simply on the defendant’s earlier act, and that understanding aligns with the APA’s cause of action in § 702 requiring a “legal wrong” or being “adversely affected or aggrieved.” Reading accrual to run at rule issuance would, as a practical matter, foreclose review for later-injured or newly formed regulated parties before they can sue, a result Congress did not clearly mandate in § 2401(a). The injury-based rule is also more workable and consistent with judicial restraint because it avoids converting § 2401(a) into a categorical immunity for longstanding but potentially unlawful rules as applied to parties who lacked any earlier opportunity to challenge them.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2401(a) starts the six-year clock when a claim “first accrues,” and in ordinary usage a claim accrues when the plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action—i.e., when the plaintiff is actually injured. The APA’s cause of action in § 702 reinforces that understanding because it authorizes suit only for a person who suffers a “legal wrong” or is “adversely affected or aggrieved,” so an uninjured party at promulgation lacks a claim to accrue. While several circuits (e.g., Dunn-McCampbell) have assumed an issuance-based rule for facial challenges, those decisions largely proceed without close attention to the statutory text and risk barring suits before they can be brought, a result difficult to square with the ordinary meaning of “accrues.” Supreme Court accrual cases emphasize claim-completeness and reject expanding limitations rules beyond the statutory language, supporting an injury-based accrual framework here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2401(a) bars suits filed more than six years after the “right of action first accrues,” and this Court’s traditional rule is that accrual occurs when the plaintiff has a “complete and present cause of action”—i.e., when the plaintiff can file suit and obtain relief. Bay Area Laundry & Dry Cleaning Pension Tr. Fund v. Ferbar Corp., 522 U.S. 192, 201 (1997). Read alongside the APA’s cause of action in 5 U.S.C. § 702—limited to persons who suffer a “legal wrong” or are “adversely affected or aggrieved”—an APA claim is not complete until the plaintiff is actually injured by the rule, so starting the clock at promulgation would unfairly extinguish claims before they exist. That injury-based reading better serves procedural fairness and preserves meaningful judicial review for later-injured parties, while concerns about regulatory repose can be addressed through ordinary merits doctrines and tailored equitable principles rather than a categorical time bar untethered to injury.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the six-year statute of limitations for an APA challenge to an agency rule begins when the rule is issued or only when the particular plaintiff is first injured/adversely affected by that rule.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2401(a) (six-year limit for civil actions against the United States, using the phrase “first accrues”), as applied to APA review under 5 U.S.C. § 702 (authorizing suit by a person who has “suffer[ed] legal wrong” or is “adversely affected or aggrieved”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Corner Post argues an APA claim cannot “first accrue” until the plaintiff has a complete and enforceable cause of action—i.e., until the plaintiff is actually injured or adversely affected by the rule—so a newly formed or newly affected business should still be able to bring a facial APA challenge within six years of its first injury, even if the rule itself is older.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Federal Reserve Board argues the claim “first accrues” at promulgation because the challenged agency action is final upon issuance and the limitations clock should run from that fixed, administrable date to protect reliance interests and regulatory finality; under this view, later-affected or newly created parties are time-barred if they sue more than six years after the rule’s issuance (absent equitable tolling).
key_precedents: The circuit split described in the Question Presented: Sixth Circuit approach (accrual upon injury/adverse effect) versus Eighth Circuit and five other circuits (accrual at rule issuance).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that, in the sovereign-immunity and rulemaking context, Congress may have wanted a fixed, administrable cutoff keyed to final agency action to protect reliance interests and avoid perpetual exposure. But § 2401(a) speaks in plaintiff-centered terms—when the “right of action first accrues”—and Justice Thomas’s point, reinforced by Bay Area Laundry as Justice Kavanaugh notes, is that accrual ordinarily requires a “complete and present cause of action,” which the APA itself (via § 702’s “adversely affected or aggrieved” limitation) withholds until someone is actually injured. Lujan’s separation of finality and injury cuts against equating “accrues” with promulgation; reading promulgation as the trigger would effectively install a statute-of-repose feature for later-injured parties without clear textual authorization. Under a minimalist approach, the government’s finality concerns are better addressed through narrow remedies and conventional equitable constraints than by adopting a categorical promulgation-based bar that the text does not clearly support.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that sovereign-immunity and administrability concerns suggest a fixed, promulgation-based cutoff akin to repose, but § 2401(a) does not speak in terms of “promulgation” or “final agency action”—it starts when the plaintiff’s “right of action first accrues,” which in ordinary legal usage means when a plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action. In the APA context, § 702 is not merely a standing overlay; it limits the very existence of a cause of action to a person “adversely affected or aggrieved,” so an uninjured (or nonexistent) party cannot have an accrued right at promulgation. Justice Alito’s reliance on Lujan v. National Wildlife Federation does not move me, because Lujan underscores that finality and injury are distinct prerequisites, reinforcing that “accrues” cannot be equated with final agency action alone. The facial/as-applied distinction may mitigate policy concerns, but as Justice Kagan notes it is not a textual basis for when the limitations clock begins, and I would not rewrite “accrues” to achieve repose-like policy ends Congress did not enact.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right to press the ordinary accrual maxim, and cases like Bay Area Laundry, Gabelli, and Wallace generally tie accrual to a plaintiff’s ability to sue; but § 2401(a) operates as a condition on the sovereign’s waiver, and in that setting it is textually plausible to read “right of action first accrues” as the first time the government’s action is complete and reviewable—i.e., upon final agency action—rather than restarting for each later-affected party. Lujan’s point (highlighted by Justice Kagan) that finality and injury are distinct prerequisites does not compel a plaintiff-by-plaintiff clock, because it addresses justiciability, not how Congress chose to set a fixed cutoff against the United States for challenges to a discrete agency act. The opposing side’s “statute of repose” characterization is more label than argument: limitations provisions frequently have repose-like consequences when they attach to an event (here, promulgation) that is the gravamen of the asserted wrong and when Congress’s evident aim is administrable finality for governmental programs. As Chief Justice Roberts suggested earlier, later-injured parties remain able to litigate concrete disputes through as-applied challenges to subsequent applications, which mitigates fairness concerns without adopting an interpretation that leaves the government perpetually exposed to facial invalidation of longstanding rules.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is administrability and reliance: a promulgation trigger supplies a clear cutoff and avoids perpetual exposure, with later parties relegated to as-applied challenges. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas explain, § 2401(a) asks when a plaintiff’s “right of action first accrues,” and under ordinary accrual doctrine a claim cannot accrue before a plaintiff exists who is “adversely affected or aggrieved” under APA § 702; otherwise we create a repose-like bar Congress did not write, shutting the courthouse door on later-injured and often vulnerable or new-entrant parties. Lujan, invoked by Justice Alito, actually underscores that finality and injury are distinct prerequisites, making it even harder to equate “accrues” with “promulgated.” Administrability and reliance can be protected through remedial limits and equitable principles—as Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh suggest—without redefining accrual to run before any justiciable claim exists.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that a promulgation trigger is administrable and protects reliance, and he argues § 2401(a) can sensibly mean the first moment an APA challenge to the rule could be brought (final agency action). But the text asks when the “right of action first accrues,” and under our ordinary accrual cases (as Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch stress, citing Bay Area Laundry) that is when this plaintiff has a complete cause of action; APA § 702 makes being “adversely affected or aggrieved” a prerequisite to having a right of action at all, so issuance-date accrual would bar suits by parties who could not have sued then, effectively adding a repose feature Congress did not write. Lujan’s separation of “final agency action” from injury/§ 702 cause-of-action prerequisites reinforces that finality alone cannot supply accrual for an uninjured plaintiff. I agree with Justice Roberts that the government’s finality concerns can be addressed through remedy/equity and, where appropriate, as-applied framing, but § 2401(a)’s accrual text cannot be rewritten to make that policy outcome categorical.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that sovereign-immunity and reliance interests suggest Congress wanted a fixed, administrable cutoff, and that “first accrues” could plausibly mean the first moment any APA challenge to the rule could be brought—at promulgation. But § 2401(a) does not speak in rule-centered terms; it starts the clock when the plaintiff’s “right of action” accrues, and as Justice Thomas explains (consistent with Bay Area Laundry, Gabelli, and Wallace), that occurs only when a plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action—something APA § 702 withholds until a person is “adversely affected or aggrieved.” Lujan, which Justice Alito invokes, underscores that final agency action is necessary but not sufficient, so equating “accrues” with “finality/promulgation” collapses distinct prerequisites and effectively creates a repose bar Congress did not write. Reliance and finality concerns are real, but as Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice now suggest, they are better addressed through remedial limits and equitable principles rather than rewriting accrual.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that § 2401(a) should provide an administrable, repose-like cutoff to protect reliance on settled regulations, with later parties limited to as-applied challenges. But the statute’s text—when the “right of action first accrues”—tracks our ordinary accrual rule (as Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett emphasize) that a claim accrues only when the plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action, and APA § 702 makes that plaintiff-specific by requiring a person “adversely affected or aggrieved.” Lujan, which Justice Alito invokes, confirms finality and injury are distinct prerequisites; it therefore cuts against equating “accrues” with promulgation and against turning § 2401(a) into a de facto statute of repose for later-injured or new entrants without clear congressional instruction. I agree with the Chief Justice’s (now revised) view that reliance and administrability concerns are better handled through remedial limits and equitable principles rather than rewriting accrual.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that § 2401(a) should function as a fixed, administrable cutoff to protect reliance interests by tying accrual to promulgation for “facial” attacks, with later parties relegated to as-applied challenges. But textually, § 2401(a) measures time from when the plaintiff’s “right of action first accrues,” and—as Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch stress—our cases treat accrual as requiring a “complete and present cause of action,” which in the APA context cannot exist until a person is “adversely affected or aggrieved” under § 702. Lujan v. National Wildlife Federation, invoked by Justice Alito, reinforces that final agency action is necessary but not sufficient; it does not support equating “accrues” with “promulgated,” and adopting that equivalence would effectively create a statute-of-repose feature Congress did not enact. The government’s finality concerns are serious, but as Chief Justice Roberts ultimately recognizes, they are better addressed through remedial limits, equitable discretion, and preclusion principles rather than rewriting accrual.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that § 2401(a) should serve as a fixed, administrable cutoff protecting reliance interests, and that later parties can still sue “as-applied.” But the text—“right of action first accrues”—tracks our ordinary, plaintiff-centered accrual rule (as Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan emphasize) and, in the APA, § 702 makes adverse effect a prerequisite to having any cause of action at all; starting the clock at promulgation would bar suit by parties who could not have sued, functioning as an atextual statute of repose. Lujan, which Justice Alito invokes, actually reinforces the separation between final agency action and a plaintiff’s entitlement to sue, undercutting the idea that finality alone can trigger accrual. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts’s concern about perpetual exposure, but I think that concern is better addressed through remedial tailoring and equitable limits rather than redefining accrual in a way that compromises procedural fairness for later-injured or newly formed parties.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 2401(a)’s six-year limit for actions against the United States is best read, for a facial challenge to a rule, to “first accrue” when the agency action becomes final and is published, providing a fixed and administrable trigger that protects reliance interests and regulatory finality. That approach aligns with the prevailing circuit view distinguishing facial challenges from later as-applied disputes, under which publication starts the clock for facial APA attacks, while later enforcement can still be litigated as-applied. Although the APA authorizes suit by one “adversely affected or aggrieved,” 5 U.S.C. § 702, that language speaks to who may sue (standing/cause of action), not to extending § 2401(a) indefinitely for new market entrants and thereby undermining institutional legitimacy and settled regulatory expectations. Federalism and separation-of-powers concerns counsel a narrow ruling preserving predictable limits on suits against the sovereign rather than adopting a rolling limitations period keyed to each plaintiff’s first injury.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 28 U.S.C. § 2401(a) starts the six-year period when the right of action “first accrues,” which, in ordinary legal usage at the time and in this Court’s cases, occurs when the plaintiff has a “complete and present cause of action”—i.e., when the plaintiff is injured and may sue. Gabelli v. SEC (quoting Wallace v. Kato) and Bay Area Laundry confirm the default rule that accrual turns on the existence of a suable claim, not merely on the defendant’s earlier conduct. Under the APA, final agency action is necessary but not sufficient; 5 U.S.C. § 702 limits suit to a person who has “suffer[ed] legal wrong” or is “adversely affected or aggrieved,” so an uninjured or nonexistent plaintiff cannot have an accrued claim at promulgation. Reading § 2401(a) to run from issuance for all “facial” challenges effectively converts a limitations statute into a statute of repose without textual warrant, contrary to the original public meaning of “accrues.”

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2401(a) provides that every civil action against the United States “shall be barred unless the complaint is filed within six years after the right of action first accrues,” and in the context of a facial challenge to a rule, that accrual is best tied to the government’s final, reviewable action—promulgation—rather than to a plaintiff-specific injury date that could extend exposure indefinitely. Although § 702 and Lujan v. National Wildlife Federation, 497 U.S. 871, 882–83 (1990), confirm that injury and finality are both necessary for a plaintiff to sue, that does not compel reading § 2401(a) to allow successive, decades-late facial challenges by newly formed entities, undermining regulatory finality and reliance interests. A promulgation-based rule provides an administrable, fixed date and avoids turning § 2401(a) into an open-ended limitations period with substantial practical consequences for government programs. Plaintiffs who first suffer injury later may still pursue as-applied challenges to subsequent agency applications, but the six-year clock for attacking the rule itself should run from issuance.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2401(a) starts the six-year clock when the plaintiff’s “right of action first accrues,” and under APA § 702 a right of action exists only for a person who has “suffer[ed] legal wrong” or been “adversely affected or aggrieved” by final agency action. Reading accrual to occur at rule issuance would bar suit by parties who could not have sued at promulgation for lack of injury, effectively converting § 2401(a) from a limitations provision into a statute of repose and undermining access to judicial review for later-affected, often vulnerable, parties. This Court’s understanding that APA review requires both final agency action and a plaintiff concretely affected—reflected in Lujan v. National Wildlife Federation, 497 U.S. 871, 882–83 (1990)—supports the commonsense rule that accrual is plaintiff-specific and begins upon first injury. Practical fairness also favors this interpretation because it prevents unlawful rules from becoming functionally unreviewable as to newly formed or newly impacted regulated entities.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2401(a) asks when a civil action “first accrues,” and in ordinary limitations doctrine a claim accrues when the plaintiff has a complete cause of action—i.e., when the plaintiff is injured and may sue. In the APA context, § 702 authorizes suit only by a person who has “suffer[ed] legal wrong” or is “adversely affected or aggrieved,” so accrual cannot sensibly occur before that plaintiff-specific injury exists, even if the agency action was final earlier. Lujan v. National Wildlife Federation underscores that final agency action and injury are distinct prerequisites; treating promulgation alone as triggering § 2401(a) effectively converts a limitations statute into a repose rule without textual warrant. Workability and reliance interests can be protected through doctrines like equitable tolling and by focusing on challenges brought within six years of a plaintiff’s first adverse effect, rather than foreclosing review for parties who did not yet exist.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2401(a) says the six-year period runs after the claim “first accrues,” and under our ordinary accrual rule a claim accrues when the plaintiff has a “complete and present cause of action,” not before. Bay Area Laundry & Dry Cleaning Pension Tr. Fund v. Ferbar Corp. confirms that default rule, and nothing in § 2401(a) clearly displaces it with a rule-triggered date keyed to promulgation. The APA’s cause of action in § 702 likewise turns on a person having “suffer[ed] legal wrong” or being “adversely affected or aggrieved,” which presupposes a plaintiff-specific injury; until then there is no justiciable claim to file. Reading accrual to occur at issuance would bar suits by later-injured parties before they ever had standing, an atextual result Congress did not clearly command in § 2401(a).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 2401(a) bars suit unless filed within six years after the “right of action first accrues,” and under this Court’s ordinary accrual rule a claim accrues only when the plaintiff has a “complete and present cause of action”—that is, when the plaintiff can file suit and obtain relief. Bay Area Laundry & Dry Cleaning Pension Tr. Fund v. Ferbar Corp. of Cal., 522 U.S. 192, 201 (1997). In the APA context, § 702 authorizes suit only by a person who has “suffer[ed] legal wrong” or is “adversely affected or aggrieved,” so a plaintiff who was not yet injured by an old rule lacks a ripe, enforceable claim and cannot have an action that has “first accrue[d].” Practical concerns about regulatory finality are real, but they cannot override the text Congress chose in § 2401(a), and they can be addressed through other doctrines (e.g., limits on remedies or equitable principles) rather than a categorical issuance-date rule.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2401(a) bars suits filed more than six years after the “right of action first accrues,” and in ordinary usage a claim accrues when the plaintiff has a “complete and present cause of action”—i.e., when the plaintiff can file suit and obtain relief. Bay Area Laundry & Dry Cleaning Pension Tr. Fund v. Ferbar Corp. confirms that default accrual rule absent contrary statutory direction, and nothing in § 2401(a) resets accrual to the defendant’s act rather than the plaintiff’s injury. Reading § 2401(a) alongside APA § 702—authorizing suit only by a person who has “suffer[ed] legal wrong” or is “adversely affected or aggrieved”—reinforces that an APA plaintiff’s claim cannot accrue until that plaintiff is actually injured or adversely affected by the rule. While reliance interests and administrability are relevant, they cannot override the enacted text; those concerns are better addressed through other doctrines (e.g., equitable limits on relief) rather than rewriting accrual to mean promulgation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2401(a) says a civil action against the United States must be filed within six years after the claim “first accrues,” and this Court’s default accrual rule is that a limitations period begins when the plaintiff has a “complete and present cause of action”—i.e., when the plaintiff can file suit and obtain relief. Under the APA, Congress limited review to a “person” who has “suffer[ed] legal wrong” or is “adversely affected or aggrieved,” 5 U.S.C. § 702, so an uninjured would-be challenger lacks a complete cause of action at promulgation. Starting the clock at issuance would deny later-injured parties any meaningful opportunity to seek judicial review, undermining procedural fairness and insulating potentially unlawful rules from review as applied to new entrants. While the government’s finality and reliance interests are real, they can be addressed through equitable doctrines and merits standards without rewriting accrual to detach it from injury.
